reference.source: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics / Rheumatology (standard texts)
clinicalPearls: The commonest subtype of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and the only one still without a confirmed molecular marker, so diagnosis remains clinical using the 2017 international criteria.

Diagnosis requires generalised joint hypermobility (assessed by the Beighton score with age-adjusted cut-offs) plus a combination of systemic connective-tissue features, positive family history and musculoskeletal complications, after exclusion of other heritable connective-tissue disorders.
Skin is soft and mildly hyperextensible with a velvety texture but, unlike classical EDS, lacks marked fragility, wide atrophic scarring or severe bruising.
Chronic widespread pain, fatigue, recurrent joint subluxations/dislocations and premature osteoarthritis are the dominant sources of morbidity.
Frequently overlaps with dysautonomia (including postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome), functional gastrointestinal disorders, and mast cell activation symptoms.
Cornerstones of management are physiotherapy for joint stabilisation and proprioception, graded exercise, pacing, and multidisciplinary chronic-pain and fatigue management rather than surgery.

In contrast to vascular EDS, life-threatening arterial or hollow-organ rupture is not a feature; however, cardiovascular assessment (including echocardiography for aortic root) is reasonable at diagnosis.
Pelvic-floor dysfunction, hernias, pelvic organ prolapse, and pregnancy-related complications are more frequent and merit anticipatory care.
reference.pathophysiology: Hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is a heritable disorder of connective tissue in which the extracellular matrix supporting joints, skin and vessels is qualitatively abnormal, producing tissue laxity and reduced tensile strength. Although inheritance appears autosomal dominant with variable expressivity and a female preponderance in clinical series, no single causative gene has been reliably identified, and the condition is presumed genetically heterogeneous, possibly involving collagen processing, minor collagens or matrix regulatory proteins. The resulting ligamentous laxity leads to recurrent joint instability, microtrauma and secondary chronic pain and osteoarthritis, while altered matrix in autonomic and visceral tissues is thought to contribute to the commonly co-occurring dysautonomia, gastrointestinal dysmotility and pelvic-floor dysfunction.
additionalDifferentials: generalised (benign) joint hypermobility without syndromic features
additionalInvestigations: Beighton score assessment with age-appropriate thresholds and application of the 2017 hEDS diagnostic criteria
genetic testing (including panels for other EDS subtypes and heritable connective-tissue disorders) primarily to exclude alternative diagnoses
transthoracic echocardiography to assess aortic root dimensions and valves
orthostatic vital signs or tilt-table testing where dysautonomia is suspected
bone density assessment where fragility or osteogenesis imperfecta is considered
targeted imaging of symptomatic joints for instability or early osteoarthritis
assessment for pelvic-floor dysfunction and hernias when indicated
redFlags: features suggesting vascular EDS (translucent skin, easy arterial/organ rupture, acrogeria) requiring urgent COL3A1 evaluation
aortic root dilatation or lens dislocation pointing towards Marfan or Loeys-Dietz syndrome
significant skin fragility with abnormal scarring suggesting classical EDS
acute severe abdominal or chest pain that could indicate a vascular or visceral catastrophe and must not be dismissed as chronic pain
reference.prognosis: Life expectancy is normal, but many patients experience chronic pain, fatigue and recurrent joint instability that can substantially impair function and quality of life; outcomes are improved by early multidisciplinary rehabilitation and self-management.
pitfalls: diagnosing hEDS on hypermobility alone without applying the full 2017 criteria or excluding other heritable connective-tissue disorders
attributing every symptom to hEDS and overlooking a treatable comorbidity or an alternative EDS subtype with vascular risk
recommending joint surgery prematurely when conservative rehabilitation is first-line and surgical outcomes are often poor in lax tissue
missing associated dysautonomia, gastrointestinal or mast cell symptoms that are amenable to specific treatment
references: 2017 International Classification of the Ehlers-Danlos Syndromes
management: The cornerstone is physiotherapy for joint stabilisation and proprioception, graded exercise and activity pacing rather than surgery
Manage chronic widespread pain multimodally with physical therapy, non-opioid analgesia and psychological pain-management support, minimising opioids
Stabilise joints with bracing, orthotics and occupational therapy, reserving surgery for selected refractory instability and anticipating poorer surgical outcomes

Treat co-occurring dysautonomia and postural orthostatic tachycardia with fluid and salt loading, compression garments and pharmacotherapy such as a beta-blocker, fludrocortisone or midodrine where needed
Manage functional gastrointestinal symptoms and mast cell activation symptoms symptomatically, using antihistamines for the latter
Screen the aortic root and valves with echocardiography and monitor as indicated
Address fatigue and provide multidisciplinary chronic-illness self-management and education, offering genetic assessment mainly to exclude other heritable connective-tissue disorders
